en: I had thought to offer in sacrifice.
I search the hills, but there are no tracks,
Nor anyone who would steal it.
Could God strike one down like this?
This beard fit to be burned,
Has it truly burned away?
Zhelmayyan, left by my Khan Manas,
Has it truly disappeared?
My child, calamity befell me and I grieved.
The enemy sheared my beard;
Today I have lost Zhelmayyan.
I have blunted my steel;
A dreadful, unbearable day befell me;
I lost Zhelmayyan.
With no cause for grief, I grieved.
A curse on old age!
The flat-humped black camel—
My child, I have lost Zhelmayyan.
My heart's support, left by Manas,
Alas, when the orphan comes,
‘My father's Zhelmayyan,
Uncle, where has it gone?’ when he asks,
With this beard of mine burning,
What calamity shall I bear?
Thus I have suffered a dark day;
What answer shall I give my child?
My fortune and prosperity blocked,
Could God strike one down like this?
Parted from Zhelmayyan,
Could my fortune shatter like this?
My child, have you seen Zhelmayyan?
Have you recognized Zhelmayyan?
My child, Zhelmayyan's distinguishing marks:
A flat-humped black camel,
On your head is a golden halter,
Its front lip is floppy,
Its rear hump flaps:
Zhelmayyan, left by Manas.
My child, these are its marks.
Have you recognized Zhelmayyan?
My child, have you heard of Zhelmayyan?
If you have seen Zhelmayyan,
I will agree to what you say.
Bek-Zhayloo at the head of Besh-Tash,
Where they had settled in hiding,
When valiant Manas passed away,
The many Kyrgyz, the numerous Argyn,
When they scattered and moved in all directions,
They were the people left by Manas.
‘Let descendants of the people remain,’
I, Bakay, was the one who tended them.
I have a people of five hundred households.
My child, I will agree to what you say.
All of them, without shaking my head in refusal,
If you have seen Zhelmayyan,
My child, I will give as a reward for good news!
Kokcholok beneath me,
My wedded wife Korpoyan,
My only son Baytaylak,
My child, I will give them too.
On the hills I have sixty thousand horses,
My swift coursers with piebald heads,
Thoroughbreds and racers mingled—
I will give these too!
My child, today God took away my strength.
I have lost, my foal,
Today, a beast such as my Zhelmayyan.”
So saying, Khan Bakay
Turned Kokcholok's head;
He kept lamenting further.
“Hiding myself in Talas,
Because of exhaustion and misery,
The orphan in Talas,
Then sending him fleeing toward Bukhara,
Because of grief,
The imposing orphan,
Sending him fleeing on foot from Keng-Kol—
If the orphan came to Talas,
I, poor soul, had been thinking:
‘Let me dedicate and sacrifice Zhelmayyan
To my departed friend Manas.’
Not even a young camel remains, let alone Zhelmayyan.
One day in seven is torment.
Were you like this, world of shit?
Hill after hill, roaming the hills,
Though Zhelmayyan is a beast,
It is a beloved companion left by my Khan Manas.
We joined in childhood,
United when louse-sized,
Companions scouting when on a journey—
Could a dark day be like this?
A beloved companion left by my Khan Manas.
I have blunted my steel;
Today I have lost Zhelmayyan!”
While Bakay stood bellowing and weeping,
Something came into his mind,
Semetey, born of your mighty Manas:
“My mother Kanykey said:
‘If you should see mighty Bakay,
He is more of a lion than your father,’ she said.
Bakay, of whom she spoke,
Let me test him further.
If Bakay is a poor creature,
Let me sacrifice him,
Have him dragged onto the road,
And tear him apart for the dogs.
Rather than let him bellow in old age,
Let me put an end to him.
If he is a lion of surpassing strength,
A hero who knew my father, Khan Manas,
If Bakay has valor,
Without killing him or making him vanish,
In my khan father's place
Let me take him as my support.
Making Bakay my guiding mark,
Let me bring slaughter upon Beijing.
Having him scout the land, learning the people,
If he truly is a hero,
Let me keep him as my inheritance.
If Bakay is a poor creature,
Let me remove him from this world,
Let me put an end to him.”
Kokcholok beneath him,
Alas, had grown thin.
Khan Bakay upon it,
Herding camels and bellowing much,
Alas, had grown old.
Bakay's appearance had deteriorated;
His eyes had begun to fester;
His chest had begun to wheeze.
Both his eyes were red;
His neck was awkwardly stretched long.
That year, Bakay
Had a goatskin coat on his body,
Leather trousers on his backside,
His beard white.
Had the boy not come then,
Your Bakay was near death.
The mount beneath him,
Having lost its mane and tail,
Had acquired the name Kokcholok.
Misfortune had struck it;
It had fallen into ill repute,
Had come to be called Kokcholok.
Testing Bakay's valor,
He turned his words another way.
The orphan lad born of Manas
Now acted as a stranger:
“Brother-in-law Bakay, you will come to no good.
Pledged to seven spiritual masters,
Your orphan Manas is not here.
Always barking out,
You will not give up your bullying.
You have no garden planted in Keng-Kol,
You arrogant brother-in-law.
This is no time for you to swagger,
No time for you to quarrel.
You have no garden established in Keng-Kol,
No time for your arrogant words.
For you to speak mockingly,
Your proud Khan Manas is gone.
Who would split it apart,
Who would put it on his trouser hems—
Your heroic Khan Manas is gone.
Do not bark, brother-in-law.
Who would oppress everyone,
Your sovereign Khan Manas is gone!
In your time of herding camels,
You will not give up your imperious ways,
Though you are at the point of death.
‘Seizing your elder sister,
I struck your whole village,’ you say,
And again you speak grandly.
‘I made your sister my wife in the wilderness,’ you say,
‘Smashing your father, Khan Janaaly,
I seized her by force,’ you say.
You speak without restraint.
Is your great Manas here?
Let me make you lose your composure;
Let me cool, old man,
That far-reaching bluster of yours.
Kokcholok beneath you,
Let me seize it now.
This rumbling old man's
Two testicles, cutting off both,
Let me make him a eunuch.
If you violated my sister,
Old man, let me take my revenge on you this way!
Old man, let me see your might.
Having a halter put upon its neck,
You ask for what you lost;
You keep saying, ‘Zhelmayyan.’
Old man, whom are you mocking?
Are the guardian Kyrgyz here?
Old man, these words of yours are bad words.
Whom are you mocking?
If your Kyrgyz make you herd camels,
They are your subjects left by Khan Manas.
Old man, Kokcholok, which you will not give if asked,
Let me take it by force.
Your Khan Manas has died;
Let me exact my long-standing vengeance from you.
Let me press down upon your head,
Let me scatter all four kinds of your livestock.
Seizing your mares,
If you come close, I will strike and scatter your brains,
Let me make you mourn
Your giant, Leopard Manas.
Then let me find for you
A camel such as your Zhelmayyan.
Let me put an end to
Those far-fetched arguments of yours.
Let me seize by force
A beast such as Kokcholok beneath you.
Let me put an end, old man,
To that far-reaching pride of yours.
Wretched old man, you will come to no good!
You will not give up your bluster!
‘I forced your sister,’ you say.
Even as you die, old man,
You will not give up your fury.
Old man, let me split your gallbladder now;
Let me see your vengeance!”
So saying, Semetey
Took the battle-axe in his hand,
Struck Aktulpar once,
Took his sword and drew himself up smartly,
Then lunged toward Bakay,
Making a sudden move.
Then Bakay said this:
“Let me turn my courser's head.
Stand there before me; do not run away.
My child, I will make your mother my wife!
Saddle-sore from herding camels,
I have a beast such as Kokcholok.
Let God strike me forty times outright;
Even if cut into eighty pieces,
My child, I have strength enough for you!
If you ask about my circumstances,
My child, alas, I herd camels.
If God strikes me four times,
My child, I will not spare you.
An inheritance entrusted by my lord,
I have beasts called camels.
Let him strike me ten times at once;
Scoundrel, I have strength enough for you.
Alas, Kokcholok beneath me,
You met it when it had grown thin.
Khan Bakay, who laid waste to this world,
You met him when he had grown old.
This river valley of Talas,
My foal, you met me when it had become my road.
Parted from my tiger,
You met me when I was disgraced.
The marten-fur cap upon my head,
You met me when it had become grass.
